snippet: The Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 1,000 confirmed Ebola cases by June 21, 2026, marking the first time since the 2018-2020 epidemic. The 2026 DRC/Uganda outbreak (magenta) had passed 1,000 confirmed cases by day 37 with no sign of slowing. Sources: WHO situation reports compiled by Caitlin Rivers (2014–2016), Kristian G. [...] The Democratic Republic of Congo surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases of Ebola as of June 21, 2026, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the first time any Ebola outbreak has crossed that threshold since the catastrophic 2018–2020 epidemic in North Kivu and Ituri. That alone would be alarming. What makes this outbreak harder to address is that it is spreading across remote, conflict-affected terrain with no vaccine available for this strain of the virus.

title: Ebola disease outbreak 2026: How MSF is responding
snippet:
In just 10 weeks, this current Ebola disease outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has become the fastest-growing outbreak on record. From July 19–26 alone, 800 additional confirmed cases were reported, and more than 400 new deaths.

Currently, more than 1,400 Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) staff are on the ground in DRC, treating patients, setting up Ebola treatment centers and isolation units, and delivering supplies to overwhelmed health facilities. [...] Unlike most Ebola disease outbreaks that have occurred in DRC, this one is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or treatment. This is the third detected outbreak involving Bundibugyo, following outbreaks in Uganda in 2007–2008 and in DRC in 2012. During the two previous outbreaks, the estimated fatality rate ranged from 25 to 40 percent.

##### Learn more about the Bundibugyo virus > [...] There are different viruses that cause the Ebola disease, named after where they were discovered: Bundibugyo, Ivory Coast, Reston, Sudan, and Ebola (also known as Zaire). While there is an approved treatment and a preventive vaccine for Zaire, there is no treatment or vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus currently spreading in DRC and Uganda. Medical teams can give patients the best chance of survival by helping to manage the symptoms of the virus and treating other diseases the patient may have.
